title: Vithya Targets Sub-54 After Smashing PT Usha's 42-Year-Old Record
excerpt: The 28-year-old hurdler became the first Indian woman under 55 seconds at Aichi-Nagoya. She says domestic competition doesn't push her — and she wants to race the world's best to go faster.
body:
• National record holder Vithya Ramraj has set her sights on breaking the 54-second barrier next, after clocking 54.75 seconds to shatter PT Usha's 42-year-old 400m hurdles record at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
  • Her coach Nehpal Singh Rathore says she can go sub-54 — he expected close to 54.5 seconds at Nagoya, and believes better competition, not easier races, will push her faster.
  • Vithya left Japan with three medals: gold in the women's 4x400m relay (3:29.69), silver in the mixed 4x400m relay (3:14.46), and bronze in the hurdles, where she became the first Indian woman under 55 seconds.
  • She told The Hindu she is "not pushed enough" at home, and wants to race top-class fields abroad — a long-standing demand from an athlete who has lacked sponsors and international exposure.

Vithya Ramraj is done chasing ghosts. Having finally erased PT Usha's 42-year-old national record in the women's 400m hurdles at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the 28-year-old from Coimbatore has a new target: a sub-54-second run. Speaking to The Hindu after returning from Japan, she said she is "not pushed enough" by domestic competition — and that only racing the world's best will carry her into the next bracket.

At Nagoya, Vithya clocked 54.75 seconds to win bronze, becoming the first Indian woman to run the 400m hurdles under 55 seconds. The run bettered Usha's 55.42, set at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics and untouched for more than four decades. Vithya had first equalled that mark at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou; this time, with Usha watching from the stands, she moved beyond it.

The night the record fell

The final tested her nerve. Rain had disrupted her warm-up in Nagoya — a genuine worry for an athlete who suffered a serious ankle injury at the Asian championships in 2025 and ran that race with swollen ankles, still winning bronze. She had also fallen over a hurdle at a Delhi meet on September 10. In the final she cleared all ten hurdles to finish third behind the UAE's Mariam Kareem, who won gold in a Games-record 54.31 seconds, and Kazakhstan's Adelina Zems, who took silver in 54.58.

https://x.com/the_hindu/status/2107946568728928647

She did not win the race, but she beat the number she had chased for three years. "I was getting upset when people kept asking me when I would run 55 or 54," she said after the race. "But I kept working. Today it happened." Before the race, her coach Nehpal Singh Rathore had stripped the pressure down to one line: chase the timing, not the medal. Usha, in the VIP arena, stood to applaud as the record fell. "Records are meant to be broken," she said.

The coach's arithmetic

Rathore, a former national-level sprinter who has coached Vithya since 2021 and holds a World Athletics coaching certification, believes the Nagoya time is a waypoint, not a ceiling. Speaking to the Times of India from Nagoya, he said he had expected her to run close to 54.5 seconds in the final — the 54.75 was good, but the plan always assumed a steeper progression. "She can go sub-54," he said.

The progression supports him. Vithya missed Usha's mark by a hundredth of a second at an Indian Grand Prix in 2023 (55.43), ran 56.04 while tired at the 2025 Federation Cup in Kochi, and then dropped to 54.75 when it mattered.

"I was getting upset when people kept asking me when I would run 55 or 54. But I kept working. Today it happened."

— Vithya Ramraj

Why she needs to be pushed

The "not pushed enough" line is a structural complaint Indian middle-distance athletes have made for years. Vithya has said before that domestic fields leave her running alone; she would need the Asian Games fields of Japan and China to find the record. She has spoken about lacking sponsors and about India having only one "B"-grade meet on the rankings ladder. The answer, she says, is racing abroad against top-class athletes — exposure that requires funding she has repeatedly had to ask for. She dedicated her bronze to her twin sister Nithya, also an athlete, who missed Japan through injury.

What's next

The immediate focus is a World Championships debut, with Vithya and her coach targeting a sub-54-second run on the global stage. If she gets there, she enters territory where Indian women's hurdling has never been — a finalist-level time at a global championship. The obstacles are logistical as much as athletic: quality races, travel support and the right competition fields. Her coach's verdict stands as the roadmap: she doesn't need easier races. She needs faster ones.
